F1.quote: The AI Incident Database is dedicated to indexing the collective history of harms or near harms realized in the real world by the deployment of artificial intelligence systems.
F1.claim: the database defined by its own home page: indexing the collective history of real-world harms or near harms from deployed AI systems
F1.lineage: what it is: indexing harms and near harms

F2.quote: Like similar databases in aviation and computer security, the AI Incident Database aims to learn from experience so we can prevent or mitigate bad outcomes.
F2.claim: its purpose, on the model of aviation and computer-security databases: learn from experience to prevent or mitigate bad outcomes
F2.lineage: purpose: a collective memory of failures, after aviation

F3.quote: You are invited to submit incident reports, whereupon submissions will be indexed and made discoverable to the world.
F3.claim: open submission: incident reports submitted are indexed and made discoverable

F4.locus: The Responsible AI Collaborative ¶1 (also B11, the same paragraph)
F4.quote: The AI Incident Database is a project of the Responsible AI Collaborative, an organization chartered to advance the AI Incident Database.
F4.claim: the operator: a project of the Responsible AI Collaborative, chartered to advance it

F5.locus: incident list (the highest id on the page, 2026-10-29)

F6.quote: The MIT AI Incident Tracker classifies 1,600 real-world report incidents from the AI Incident Database by risk, cause, harm, severity, and other relevant dimensions.
F6.claim: MIT's tracker classifies 1,600 AIID incidents by risk, cause, harm and severity (the card snippet gives 1,752; the page's meta description 'more than 1,400')
F6.lineage: derived layer: MIT AI Incident Tracker

F7.locus: What is the AI Incident Tracker? ¶1
F7.quote: Raw reports from the AI Incident Database (AIID) are processed by Arcola AI's LLM pipeline, which categorizes them using established frameworks, such as the MIT Risk Repository and a harm severity rating system based on CSET’s AI Harm Taxonomy.
F7.claim: the tracker's method: AIID raw reports processed by Arcola AI's LLM pipeline against the MIT Risk Repository and a CSET-based severity scale
F7.lineage: derived layer: MIT AI Incident Tracker

F8.locus: What is the AI Incident Tracker? ¶3
F8.quote: We build on the great work done by the Responsible AI Collaborative who created and maintain the AI Incident Database, reviewing all submitted reports and ensuring the quality of the dataset.
F8.claim: MIT credits the Responsible AI Collaborative with creating and maintaining the database and reviewing all submitted reports

F9.locus: Limitations of the analysis and dataset
F9.quote: As the reporting is voluntary, the dataset is inevitably subject to some degree of sampling bias. … a systematic validation study has not yet been completed.
F9.claim: the tracker's stated limits: voluntary reporting gives sampling bias; no systematic validation study yet
F9.lineage: derived layer: MIT AI Incident Tracker

F10.locus: Workstreams / Safety Critical AI / AI Incident Database, Overview ¶1–2
F10.quote: The AI Incident Database (AIID) is a tool designed to help us better imagine and anticipate these risks, collecting more than 1,200 reports of intelligent systems causing safety, fairness, or other real-world problems. … As a central, systematized repository of problems experienced in the real world as a result of AI, this crowdsourced database can help AI practitioners mitigate or avoid repeated bad outcomes in the future.
F10.claim: Partnership on AI's workstream page: a tool to anticipate risks, more than 1,200 reports, a crowdsourced central repository
F10.lineage: what it is: indexing harms and near harms

F11.quote: As AI technology is integrated into an increasing number of safety-critical systems — entering domains such as transportation, healthcare, and energy — the potential impact of this technology’s failures similarly grows.

F11.lineage: purpose: a collective memory of failures, after aviation

F20.claim: the issue defined: a harm or near harm that has yet to occur or be detected
F20.lineage: the unit: incident, report, issue, variant

F21.quote: The AIID editorial record that bounds and summarizes a specific harmful or near-harm event or traceable episode.
F21.claim: the incident ID defined: the editorial record bounding and summarizing an event
F21.lineage: the unit: incident, report, issue, variant

F22.quote: A source document attached to an incident ID. Multiple reports may document the same underlying event.
F22.claim: the report defined: a source document attached to an incident ID; several may document one event
F22.lineage: the unit: incident, report, issue, variant

F23.quote: A report is evidence; an incident ID is the database’s normalized account of an event. A later source about the same underlying event is usually an additional report, not a new incident.
F23.claim: report is evidence, incident ID the normalized account; a later source on the same event is usually an additional report
F23.lineage: the unit: incident, report, issue, variant

F24.quote: A distinct incident involving the same intelligent system, substantially similar causative factors, and substantially similar harms as a known incident.
F24.claim: the variant defined: a distinct incident, same system, substantially similar causes and harms
F24.lineage: the unit: incident, report, issue, variant

F25.quote: The database records publicly documented allegations of harm or near harm. It does not independently adjudicate every factual claim.
F25.claim: governing principle: it records publicly documented allegations and does not adjudicate every factual claim
F25.lineage: what it represents and its limits

F26.quote: 1. IS THERE A SPECIFIC EVENT? … 2. IS AN AI SYSTEM IDENTIFIABLE? … 3. IS THE AI SYSTEM CAUSALLY IMPLICATED? … 4. IS THERE HARM OR CREDIBLE NEAR HARM? … 5. IS THE EVIDENCE ADEQUATE?
F26.claim: inclusion by five questions: specific event, identifiable AI system, causal implication, harm or credible near harm, adequate evidence

F27.quote: At least one source must support the essential event, and uncertainty must be expressible without turning the record into speculation.
F27.claim: the evidence condition: at least one source supports the essential event

F28.quote: An AI system is implicated when it played an important role in the chain of events that produced the alleged harm. It need not be the sole or dominant cause.
F28.claim: implication defined: an important role in the chain of events, not necessarily sole or dominant

F29.quote: A near-harm event exists when the system helped create a chain of events that could readily have produced harm but an external factor prevented the outcome. The external factor must be independent of the system and should not simply be a built-in safeguard functioning as designed.
F29.claim: near harm defined: a chain that could readily have produced harm, prevented by an external factor independent of the system

F30.quote: General criticism of a product or technology class without identified harm. … Benchmark failures, model errors, or hallucinations that remain inside testing or private drafting and have no consequential use. … These are presumptions rather than absolute prohibitions.
F30.claim: presumptive exclusions, among them general criticism without identified harm and failures that stay inside testing; presumptions, not prohibitions

F31.quote: A retired entity or incident identifier redirected to the canonical record that replaced it.
F31.claim: duplicate mapping: a retired identifier redirected to its canonical record

F32.quote: The AIID is a curated archive of publicly documented incidents, issues, reports, and responses. … It is not a neutral mirror of all AI harms, a comprehensive denominator for risk rates, or an independent adjudication of every event.
F32.claim: a curated archive of publicly documented incidents, not a neutral mirror, denominator or adjudication
F32.lineage: what it represents and its limits

F33.quote: Wealthy countries, prominent companies, spectacular events, and English-language reporting are likely to be overrepresented. Harms affecting marginalized groups, occurring inside private organizations, or unfolding as ordinary administration may be underrepresented.
F33.lineage: what it represents and its limits

F34.quote: A lack of records is not evidence that a sector or country has no incidents.
F34.claim: absence of records is not evidence of absence of incidents
F34.lineage: what it represents and its limits
